webcrypto.name: Web Crypto API
webcrypto.description: Native Ed25519 support in your browser
webcrypto.why: This is the technology that creates your keys. If your browser supports it natively, address generation is up to 125x faster than alternatives.

csprng.name: Random Number Generator
csprng.why: Your private key is essentially a giant random number. If the randomness is weak or predictable, someone could guess your key. This test makes sure the random generator works correctly.

entropy.name: Randomness Quality
entropy.why: We generate 10,000 random numbers and check if they're evenly distributed — like rolling a fair dice thousands of times. If some numbers come up way more often, something is wrong.

network.name: Zero Network Traffic
network.description: No data leaves your browser during key generation
network.why: The most important check: we verify that absolutely nothing is sent to the internet while keys are being generated. Your private key should never leave your device.

csp.name: Security Headers
csp.description: Content Security Policy restricts data exfiltration
csp.why: Even if malicious code were injected, these browser-level rules block it from sending data anywhere. Think of it as a firewall built into the website itself.

worker.name: Worker Isolation
worker.description: Key generation runs in isolated background threads
worker.why: Your keys are created in separate "workers" — isolated mini-programs that run in the background. They can't access the main page and can't be tampered with by browser extensions.

integrity.name: Code Integrity
integrity.description: SHA-256 fingerprints match all published forge workers
integrity.why: We hash every key-generation worker (Solana, EVM, Bitcoin, Tron, Aptos, Sui) and compare each to worker-hash.json from the open build. If they match, the code hasn't been tampered with.

keygen.name: Key Generation Test
keygen.description: Generate and validate an actual Ed25519 keypair
keygen.why: The final proof: we create a real key, sign a message with it, then verify the signature. If this works, your browser can securely generate Solana addresses.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.description: Answers across every forge — patterns, modes, security, proof links, CLI, and day-to-day usage. Use the submenu to jump by topic.

what.a: A cryptocurrency address that contains a pattern you choose — for example starting with `VANI` on Solana or `0xcafe` on EVM. It is cosmetic branding on top of a normal keypair.

fake.a: No. Every forge produces standard keys for that chain. Import into a matching wallet and they work like any randomly generated address — they just look intentional.

which.a: Nine web forges — Solana, EVM, Bitcoin, Tron, Aptos, Sui, TON, Cardano, XRP — plus `npx vanitas` for the terminal. See [How it works → Chains](/how-it-works#chains).

howLong.q: How long will my pattern take?
howLong.a: Expected attempts grow exponentially with length and alphabet size. Hex (16 chars) is denser than Base58 (~58). Use the on-page difficulty estimate; start with 3–4 characters before chasing long brands.

prefixSuffix.q: Can I use prefix and suffix together?
prefixSuffix.a: Yes — both constraints multiply difficulty. Prefer one strong side (prefix or suffix) unless you have time and hash rate to spare.

produce.q: What does the Solana forge produce?
produce.a: Ed25519 keypairs as Base58 addresses (same family as Phantom / Solflare). Export as Solana CLI JSON byte arrays for easy import.

walletMint.a: Same cryptography. **Wallet** is for personal addresses; **Mint** is labeled for launchpad custom-mint fields (pump.fun, Raydium, Meteora, …). Open [/sol?mode=mint](/sol?mode=mint).

base58.q: Why can’t I use 0, O, I, or l?
base58.a: Base58 excludes look-alike characters. Patterns containing them can never appear in a real Solana address.

pump.q: Do mints need to end with “pump”?
pump.a: No. That suffix is marketing, not a protocol rule. Any valid Base58 vanity pattern works if the launchpad accepts a custom mint keypair.

networks.q: Which networks does an EVM vanity key work on?
networks.a: All EVM-compatible chains share the same address derivation. One key → one `0x` address on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, BSC, Polygon, Avalanche C-Chain, and others.

modes.q: What are wallet, CREATE, and CREATE2 modes?
modes.a:
**Wallet** — vanity EOA address.
**CREATE** — vanity address of the first contract from that key (nonce 0).
**CREATE2** — grind salt (fixed deployer) or grind deployer (fixed salt) given an init code hash.

bnb.q: Do I need a separate BNB generator?
bnb.a: No for BNB Smart Chain (EVM). Old Beacon Chain `bnb1` bech32 addresses are out of scope.

types.a: Mainnet legacy `1…`, SegWit `bc1q…`, and Taproot `bc1p…`. Export includes compressed WIF.

leading.q: Do I type the leading 1 / bc1q myself?
leading.a: Optional. The UI auto-prepends the fixed version / HRP when your prefix does not already include it.

lightning.a: Out of scope — forge addresses, not BOLTs.

get.q: What do I get from the Tron forge?
get.a: Mainnet Base58Check `T…` addresses from secp256k1 keys — wallet or CREATE (nonce 0). Leading `T` is added automatically for prefixes.

case.q: Why does a lowercase case-sensitive prefix never find?
case.a: After `T`, the next character is almost always uppercase or a digit. Leave case sensitivity off unless you need an exact case match. Base58 also excludes O, I, l.

differ.q: How do Aptos and Sui differ?
differ.a: Both use Ed25519 and hex addresses, but hashing differs: Aptos uses `sha3-256(pubkey ‖ 0x00)`; Sui uses `blake2b-256(0x00 ‖ pubkey)`. Keys are not interchangeable across ecosystems.

wallets.a: Aptos: Petra, Martian, and similar. Sui: Sui Wallet, Suiet, and others that accept hex private keys.

ton.a: Non-bounceable (`UQ…`) vs bounceable (`EQ…`) user-friendly forms of Wallet v4R2. Matching is case-sensitive.

cardano.q: What Cardano address type is forged?
cardano.a: Enterprise mainnet `addr1…` (CIP-19 type 6 — payment key only, no stake delegation in the address).

xrp.q: Is XRP the same Base58 as Bitcoin?
xrp.a: No. XRPL classic addresses use a different Base58 alphabet. Vanitas encodes `r…` classics from secp256k1 keys.

store.q: Do you store my private keys?
store.a: No. Keys never leave the browser memory of your session. See the [Security](/security) page for architecture and threat model.

verify.a:
1. DevTools → Network while mining — no key traffic
2. Airplane mode after load
3. [Live audit](/audit) + worker hash compare

weaker.a: No. Private keys still have full CSPRNG entropy. Only the public encoding is filtered.

extensions.a: Extensions can still snoop on a page. For high-value keys use a clean profile, the CLI, or an offline machine. Details: [Security → Browser](/security#browser).

report.a: Private GitHub Security Advisories — never public issues. See [Security → Disclose](/security#disclose).

proof.a: A shareable [/proof](/proof) link with address + pattern (and optional stats). Anyone can verify the match client-side. Private keys are never included.

cli.q: How do I run the CLI?
cli.a: `npx vanitas` for a wizard, or flags like `npx vanitas sol --prefix Ace --threads 8`. Supports the same deploy modes as the web app (mint, CREATE, CREATE2 flags).

import.q: How do I import into Phantom / MetaMask / etc.?
import.a: Use the export format for that forge: Solana JSON for Phantom/Solflare, hex for most EVM wallets, WIF for many Bitcoin wallets, chain-specific hex/Base58 elsewhere. Always do a tiny test transfer first.

pause.a: You can stop anytime; resume is a fresh search (no checkpoint of prior attempts).

disabled.a: Empty pattern, invalid characters for that alphabet, or pattern too long. Fix the validation message under the inputs.

freeze.a: Lower the thread count. Workers should keep the UI alive, but saturating every core on a small laptop can still feel sluggish.

faq.stillStuckBody: Deep technical detail lives in How it works. Trust model and threat notes live on Security. Integrity checks live on Audit.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.description: A full tour of Vanitas: how vanity mining works, what each forge produces, how workers search in parallel, and how to verify that nothing leaves your machine.

overview.title: What Vanitas is
overview.p1: **Vanitas** is a client-side multi-chain vanity address forge. You choose a prefix and/or suffix; the app searches for a keypair whose public address matches that pattern. Generation runs in **Web Workers on your CPU**. Private keys are created in memory on your device and are never uploaded.
overview.p2: A vanity address is still a normal cryptographic address. The private key is random; only the public encoding is filtered until it looks the way you want — useful for branding, donations, mints, and memorable public wallets.

pipeline.title: The search loop
pipeline.intro: Every forge follows the same high-level loop, repeated millions of times:
pipeline.whySecure: Searching for a vanity address does **not** weaken the private key. You are rejecting candidates until the public address looks right — the same process as generating random keys and keeping the lucky one.

reminder.label: Reminder
reminder.body: Save your private key before closing the tab. Lost keys cannot be recovered. For large balances: test with a small transfer first, prefer hardware wallets for long-term custody, and never paste keys into untrusted sites.

where.label: Where
where.note: Static hosting only; mining makes no network calls

forges.label: Forges
forges.note: Solana · EVM · Bitcoin · Tron · Aptos · Sui · TON · Cardano · XRP

output.label: Output
output.note: Export formats depend on the forge (JSON, hex, WIF, …)

pipeline.title: The search loop
steps: Draw a cryptographically secure random private key (`crypto.getRandomValues`).
Derive the public key with the chain's curve (Ed25519 or secp256k1).
Encode the address the way that chain expects (Base58, hex, bech32, …).
Compare against your prefix / suffix (and mode rules).
On match: stop workers, show the result, optional sound / proof / export.
pipeline.workersNote: Workers run this loop in parallel across CPU cores. The UI thread stays responsive; progress (attempts, rate, ETA) is aggregated from worker messages. When one worker finds a hit, the pool is terminated.

patterns.title: Difficulty, alphabets, warnings
patterns.intro: Expected time scales with pattern length and alphabet size. Each extra character multiplies the search space. The forge UI shows a live difficulty estimate based on your pattern and a measured or assumed hash rate.

base58.label: Base58
base58.note: Solana, Tron, XRP (XRPL alphabet), Bitcoin legacy

hex.label: Hex
hex.note: EVM, Aptos, Sui — case-insensitive for matching

bech32.label: Bech32
bech32.note: Bitcoin SegWit/Taproot, Cardano — fixed HRP, then charset

traps: **EVM** — only hex after `0x`. Letters beyond `a–f` are invalid.
**Tron** — addresses start with `T`; the next character is usually uppercase. Case-sensitive lowercase prefixes often never match.
**Prefix + suffix** — both constraints multiply difficulty. Start short; grow the pattern once you know your rate.

chains.title: Every forge, explained
chains.intro: Nine forges share the same UX pattern — pick a mode, set a pattern, start workers — but each chain uses different curves, hashes, and address encodings.
chains.sol: Ed25519 keypairs encoded as Base58 (32-byte public key). Native Web Crypto Ed25519 is used when the browser supports it; otherwise a WASM fallback (`watsign`). Modes: **wallet** and **mint** — same key math; mint framing is for launchpad custom-mint flows. Export: Solana CLI JSON byte array.
chains.evm: secp256k1 → uncompressed pubkey → keccak-256 → last 20 bytes → `0x…` address. One private key yields the same address on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, BSC, Polygon, and every other EVM network. Modes: wallet (EOA), CREATE at nonce 0, CREATE2 (grind salt or grind deployer). See Modes below.
chains.btc: secp256k1. Three address types: legacy P2PKH (`1…`), native SegWit P2WPKH (`bc1q…`), Taproot P2TR (`bc1p…`). Export includes WIF (compressed) for wallet import. Leading HRP / version byte is handled for you when typing prefixes.
chains.tron: Same secp256k1 + keccak path as EVM for the 20-byte account ID, then Base58Check with version byte `0x41` → `T…`. Modes: wallet and CREATE (nonce 0), using the same RLP layout as EVM then Tron encoding.
chains.aptos: Ed25519. Address = `sha3-256(pubkey ‖ 0x00)` as hex. Compatible with Petra, Martian, and other Aptos wallets that import hex secrets.
chains.sui: Ed25519. Address = `blake2b-256(0x00 ‖ pubkey)` as hex (flag byte marks the scheme). Import into Sui Wallet / Suiet with the hex private key.
chains.ton: Ed25519 + Wallet contract v4R2. Addresses are user-friendly Base64url forms: `UQ…` (non-bounceable) and `EQ…` (bounceable). Matching is case-sensitive. Import into Tonkeeper / MyTonWallet.
chains.cardano: Ed25519 enterprise address (CIP-19 type 6, payment key only): header `0x61` + Blake2b-224 payment hash, bech32 with HRP `addr` → `addr1…`.
chains.xrp: secp256k1 compressed pubkey → RIPEMD160(SHA256) account ID → XRPL classic Base58 Check → `r…`. Note: XRPL uses a different Base58 alphabet than Bitcoin.

modes.title: Wallet, mint, CREATE, CREATE2
modes.solMint: Cryptographically identical to a wallet keypair. Launchpads ask for a custom mint keypair / private key; Vanitas labels the result as mint so the export matches that workflow. Open [/sol?mode=mint](/sol?mode=mint), find a pattern, paste the key into pump.fun, Raydium, Meteora, etc.
modes.create: The first contract deployed from an EOA with nonce 0 has a deterministic address: `keccak256(RLP([sender, 0]))[12:]`. Vanitas grinds EOAs until that derived contract address matches your pattern. You receive the deployer private key — deploy once from a fresh nonce-0 account.
modes.create2Intro: Address = `keccak256(0xff ‖ deployer ‖ salt ‖ initCodeHash)[12:]`. Two grind strategies:
modes.create2Salt: **create2-salt** — fix deployer key + init code hash; search for a salt that yields the vanity address.
modes.create2Deployer: **create2-deployer** — fix salt + init code hash; search for a deployer key whose CREATE2 address matches.
modes.create2Hash: You must supply a correct `initCodeHash` (keccak of the deployment bytecode). Wrong hash → wrong on-chain address.

workers.title: Performance architecture
workers.intro: Worker sources live under `src/workers/*.worker.source.ts` and are bundled with esbuild into `public/*-worker.js`. Each build writes SHA-256 digests to `public/worker-hash.json` for the [live audit](/audit).

parallelism.label: Parallelism
parallelism.note: Adjust threads if the machine heats up or the UI stutters

libraries.label: Libraries
libraries.note: Audited pure-JS / WASM crypto in the browser

workers.postFind: After a find, optional **key security checks** probe entropy, CSPRNG availability, and a chi-square uniformity test on random bytes — confirming the browser RNG path looks healthy.

proof.title: Proof of find
proof.p1: **Share proof** builds a public link to [/proof](/proof) with chain, address, and pattern only — **never the private key**. Anyone can open the link and verify the address matches the claimed prefix/suffix client-side.
proof.session: Recent finds in the UI use `sessionStorage` for address + pattern metadata only. Closing the tab clears that history; keys are not stored there.

cli.title: Terminal forge
cli.p1: Same idea outside the browser: `npx vanitas` opens a wizard, or pass flags for chain, mode, prefix, threads, and CREATE2 parameters. Results write a JSON file with mode `0600` when the OS supports it. Package: [npmjs.com/package/vanitas](https://www.npmjs.com/package/vanitas).

verify.title: Confirm it yourself
steps: Open DevTools → Network, clear the log, start a forge — you should see **no requests** while mining.
Load the page, go offline, generate again — it still works.
Run the [live audit](/audit) and compare worker hashes to `worker-hash.json`.
Read the source on [GitHub](https://github.com/bytebrox/vanitas) — especially `src/workers/`.

security.title: Security
security.description: Keys are generated in your browser, never on our servers. This page is the trust model: architecture, threats, crypto, headers, and how to verify every claim yourself.

principles.title: Non-negotiables
principles.marketing: Marketing claims are worthless without checks. Use the [live audit](/audit) and the Verify section below.

architecture.title: Where keys live
architecture.keysRam: Private keys exist only here — RAM on your device

principles.title: Non-negotiables
items: **Client-side generation** — Web Workers on your CPU create every keypair.
**Zero key transit** — there is no API that accepts or returns private keys.
**Zero key storage** — no database, no logs of secrets, no analytics of patterns or addresses.
**Verifiable** — open source, live audit, offline test, Network panel.
**Proof without exposure** — shareable proofs carry address + pattern only.

architecture.title: Where keys live
architecture.intro: Vanitas is a static Next.js site. The host (e.g. Vercel) serves HTML, CSS, JS, and prebuilt worker bundles. Cryptography never runs on that host for your keys.
architecture.networkBody: None required. After assets load, airplane mode still works. The only first-party API route (`/api/domains`) suggests Solana domain links — it does not generate or receive keys.
architecture.serversBody: Deliver files. Cannot read your Worker memory. Cannot intercept a finished keypair. A compromised origin could serve malicious JS — that is why integrity checks and open source matter (see Integrity & Browser).

threats.title: Threat model (honest)
inScope: Server-side key theft (no keys on server).
Casual network sniffing during mining (no key traffic).
Clickjacking of the main app (frame deny on primary routes).
Obvious XSS exfiltration paths (CSP; still not a silver bullet).
outScope: **Malicious browser extensions** that read page memory or clipboard — disable them on a clean profile when forging high-value keys.
**Compromised device / malware** — OS-level keyloggers beat any website.
**You pasting keys into Discord / phishing** — operational security is yours.
**Supply-chain of dependencies** — we pin and audit; you can verify worker hashes and rebuild from source.
threats.vanityNote: Vanity mining does not create a “weaker” key. Long patterns only cost more CPU — they do not reduce private-key entropy.

storage.title: What we store
storage.intro: **Nothing about your keys on our servers.** No database of addresses, patterns, IPs for mining, or analytics SDKs in the forge path.
items: No private keys on disk or server
No public keys / addresses collected remotely
No third-party analytics in the product promise
sessionStorage recent finds = address + pattern only, this browser session
Proof links = query params you choose to share (no keys)

sol.label: Solana

crypto.postFind: Post-find checks can validate entropy size, CSPRNG presence, and chi-square uniformity on a random sample — a health check of the RNG path, not a substitute for device hygiene.

integrity.title: Workers & published hashes
integrity.p1: Mining code ships as static `public/*-worker.js` files built from TypeScript sources. Each production build records SHA-256 digests in `worker-hash.json`. The audit page re-hashes the workers your browser loaded and compares them to that file.
integrity.p2: If hashes diverge, treat the page as untrusted — stop, do not use keys, and investigate (wrong deploy, cache, or tampering). Rebuilding from the open repo should reproduce the same worker bytes for a given commit.

headers.title: HTTP security headers
headers.intro: Responses include headers that reduce XSS impact, force HTTPS, and block framing of the main app. CSP still allows what Next.js needs (including some inline / eval tradeoffs) — headers help; they do not replace code review.

browser.title: What the browser can still do
browser.intro: Anything that runs with page privileges can, in theory, read the DOM and Worker messages. That includes:
items: Browser extensions with broad site access
DevTools open on a shared machine
Malicious injected scripts if XSS exists
Clipboard sniffers after you copy a key
browser.mitigations: Mitigations: clean browser profile, no unnecessary extensions, prefer download files over clipboard for high-value keys, wipe clipboard after paste into a wallet, consider the terminal CLI or an air-gapped machine for large treasuries.

workflow.title: Safe operating procedure
steps: Load vanitas.fun (or run from a verified local build).
Optional: open Network, go offline, run audit.
Choose a short pattern first; increase length once you trust the setup.
On find: export, store offline, never screenshot keys into chat apps.
Import into the correct wallet for that chain; send a dust test transfer.
For long-term holdings, move funds to a hardware wallet — Vanitas is a forge, not a vault.

network.title: Network monitor
steps: DevTools → Network → clear
Start generating
Confirm **zero** requests while mining

offline.title: Airplane mode
steps: Load the app
Disconnect
Generate — success proves no live server dependency

audit.title: Live audit + source
steps: Run [/audit](/audit)
Compare worker hashes to published JSON
Review [GitHub](https://github.com/bytebrox/vanitas) workers and SECURITY.md

disclose.title: Reporting issues
disclose.intro: Do **not** open public GitHub issues for security vulnerabilities. Prefer private GitHub Security Advisories on [bytebrox/vanitas](https://github.com/bytebrox/vanitas/security/advisories/new). Include reproduction steps, impact, and a suggested fix if you have one.

steal.a: We have no server-side path that receives them. A malicious build or extension could — verify hashes and use a clean environment for high value.

host.q: What if the host is hacked?
host.a: Attackers could serve altered JavaScript. That is why open source, worker-hash checks, and preferring a known-good commit matter. The host still never receives your finished keys from a clean build.

weaker.a: No. Private-key entropy is unchanged. Only the public address is filtered for appearance.

cold.q: Should I forge cold-storage keys in a daily browser?
cold.a: For significant funds: clean profile or offline/CLI, small test transfer, then hardware wallet custody.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.intro: These terms govern your use of Vanitas (vanitas.fun), the related open-source code, and the optional CLI. By using the site or tools, you agree to them.

sections.title: What Vanitas is
sections.body: Vanitas is a **client-side vanity address forge**. Cryptographic work runs in your browser (or locally via the CLI). We do not operate a custodial wallet, exchange, or account system.

sections.title: No warranties
sections.body: The software is provided **as is**, without warranty of any kind. Patterns, difficulty estimates, and proofs of find are convenience features — verify results yourself before moving funds.

sections.title: Your responsibility
sections.body: You are solely responsible for safeguarding private keys, seed phrases, and exports. Anyone with a private key controls the corresponding funds. Do not share keys. Do not forge addresses for fraud, impersonation, or other unlawful use.

sections.title: Acceptable use
sections.body: Do not abuse the site infrastructure (for example automated scraping that harms availability), attempt to break security controls, or misrepresent Vanitas as a hosted key service.

sections.title: Open source & third parties
sections.body: Source is published under the MIT license on [GitHub](https://github.com/bytebrox/vanitas). Third-party wallets, explorers, npm, and hosting providers have their own terms. Links to them are for convenience only.

sections.title: Limitation of liability
sections.body: To the fullest extent permitted by law, the authors and operators are not liable for lost keys, lost funds, downtime, incorrect patterns, or damages arising from use of Vanitas.

sections.title: Changes
sections.body: We may update these terms. Continued use after a posted update constitutes acceptance of the revised terms. The date above shows the latest revision.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: Vanitas is built so private keys and generation work stay on your device. This page explains what little we touch and what we do not collect.

sections.title: Keys never leave this device
sections.body: Address forging runs **locally in your browser** (Web Workers) or in the local CLI. Vanitas does not upload private keys, mnemonics, or generated key material to our servers. **Share proof** links intentionally exclude private keys.

sections.title: What we do not collect
sections.body: We do not require accounts. We do not intentionally collect wallet balances, forged private keys, or pattern search results on a Vanitas backend. There is no Vanitas login.

sections.title: Data on your device
sections.body: Preferences such as **theme** (light/dark) may be stored in localStorage and a first-party **theme cookie** so the correct mode can render without a flash. Sound preference and similar UI state may also stay in local storage. **Recent finds** are kept in sessionStorage on your device for that browser session and are not sent to us.

sections.title: Hosting & logs
sections.body: The website is served via standard web hosting (currently Vercel). Like most sites, infrastructure may process technical request data (for example IP address, user agent, URLs, timestamps) in access logs for security and reliability. We do not use that to build marketing profiles of forged keys.

sections.title: No advertising trackers
sections.body: Vanitas does not embed third-party advertising pixels. If that changes, this policy will be updated.

sections.title: External links
sections.body: Links to explorers (for example Solscan), GitHub, npm, or social profiles are third-party sites with their own privacy practices.

sections.title: Children
sections.body: The tools are not directed at children. Do not use Vanitas if you are not legally allowed to use cryptographic wallet software in your jurisdiction.

sections.title: Contact
sections.body: Privacy questions: [Bytebrox on X](https://x.com/bytebrox) or [GitHub](https://github.com/bytebrox/vanitas). Also see [Terms](/terms) and [Security](/security).
